items.readable_text:
Content:
The difference of two sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] denoted by [MATH: A \setminus B] or [MATH: A - B,] is the set of all elements belonging to [MATH: A] and not belonging to [MATH: B.]

Content:
For example, consider the sets [MATH: A = \{ a,b,c \}] and [MATH: B = \{ b, d, e \}.] We can represent these sets using a Venn diagram, as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3b24a58f2bd23f1d2f6fb8314b8cf718]

Content:
The difference [MATH: A \setminus B] consists of all the elements that are in [MATH: A] but not [MATH: B.] To represent [MATH: A \setminus B,] we will shade in all the area that is contained within [MATH: A] but not [MATH: B.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/312a882ebe17f19513ce47914d28c37c]

Content:
The elements [MATH: a] and [MATH: c] are contained in [MATH: A] but not [MATH: B.] Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: A \setminus B = A - B = \{ a,c \}.]

Content:
Note: The difference can be defined using set-builder notation as follows:

Content:
[MATH: A \setminus B = A - B = \{ x \mid x \in A \text { and } x \notin B \}]

Content:
The condition "[MATH: x \in A \text { and } x \notin B]" means that [MATH: x] must belong to [MATH: A] but [MATH: x] must not belong to [MATH: B.]

Item 6 — Example: Finding a Difference of Sets Without a Venn Diagram

Example Prompt:
Given the sets [MATH: X = \{ 2, 5, 7, 8 \},] [MATH: Y = \{ 1, 3, 5 \},] and [MATH: Z = \{ 2, 4, 6, 8 \},] find [MATH: X \setminus Y,] [MATH: Y \setminus Z,] and [MATH: Z \setminus X.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The set [MATH: X \setminus Y] is the set of all elements belonging to [MATH: X] but not [MATH: Y.] Note that the element [MATH: 5 \in Y] is also in [MATH: X,] so we must remove it. Hence, we have

[MATH: X∖Y|= X − Y; = {2, 5, 7, 8} − {1, 3, 5}; = {2, 7, 8}.]

The set [MATH: Y \setminus Z] is the set of all elements belonging to [MATH: Y] but not [MATH: Z.] Note that none of the elements of [MATH: Y] are in [MATH: Z.] So, we have

[MATH: Y∖Z|= Y − Z; = {1, 3, 5} − {2, 4, 6, 8}; = {1, 3, 5}.]

The set [MATH: Z \setminus X] is the set of all elements belonging to [MATH: Z] but not [MATH: X.] Note that the elements [MATH: 2,8 \in Z] are also in [MATH: X,] so we must remove them. Therefore, we have

[MATH: Z∖X|= Z − X; = {2, 4, 6, 8} − {2, 5, 7, 8}; = {4, 6}.]

Item 9 — Example: Finding Differences of Sets Given Verbally

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: A] be the set of all multiples of [MATH: 4] that are greater than [MATH: 0] and let [MATH: B] be the set of all multiples of [MATH: 6] that are greater than [MATH: 0.] What is [MATH: A \setminus B?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The multiples of [MATH: 4] that are greater than [MATH: 0] are

[MATH: A = \{ 4,8,12,16,20,24,28,32, 36 \ldots \}.]

Likewise, multiples of [MATH: 6] that are greater than [MATH: 0] are

[MATH: B = \{ 6,12,18,24,30,36,\ldots \}.]

Now, [MATH: A \setminus B] is the difference of [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] which means that we want to find the elements that are in [MATH: A] but not in [MATH: B.]

The elements of [MATH: A] that are also in [MATH: B] are [MATH: 12, 24, 36] and so on (i.e. multiples of [MATH: 12]). So, we must remove these elements from [MATH: A.] Therefore, we have

[MATH: A∖B|= A − B; = {4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, …} − {6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, …}; = {4, 8, 16, 20, 28, 32, …}.]
